COVERAGE DROP CHECK · RUNS IN YOUR BROWSER

Did this PR drop your coverage?

Paste the Cobertura or JaCoCo XML from main (or the last release) and from this pull request. This page subtracts the two line-coverage rates and lists every file that got worse, better, new, or removed.

A floor such as --cov-fail-under=80 will let a PR drop from 92% to 81% and still pass. This check answers the delta, not the floor. Nothing is uploaded.

1. Get two coverage XML reports

Anything that writes Cobertura or JaCoCo XML works:

pytest --cov --cov-report=xml:baseline.xml     # then again on the PR for current.xml
coverage xml                                    # coverage.py, writes coverage.xml
nyc report --reporter=cobertura --report-dir .  # Istanbul / nyc
mvn test                                        # JaCoCo writes target/site/jacoco/jacoco.xml

Keep the baseline from the same suite and the same tool. Mixing a Cobertura report with a JaCoCo report is fine — both are reduced to line covered / line valid — but mixing different test sets is not.

2. Paste baseline and current

Paste both reports and click "Compare coverage". Default allowance is 0 — any drop fails.

Verdict

Prefer a CLI, or want this as a CI gate?

Same logic, zero dependencies, one file:

python3 check.py baseline.xml current.xml            # exits 1 if coverage dropped
python3 check.py baseline.xml current.xml --max-drop 0.5
python3 check.py baseline.xml current.xml --json

Get check.py from the repo — stdlib only, nothing to install. It reads local files and makes no network call.

Common questions

How is a drop decided?

The overall line-coverage rate on the baseline report minus the same rate on the current report, in percentage points. If that number is greater than the allowance (default: any drop), the check fails. That is arithmetic on the two reports, not a guess and not a comparison against a fixed floor such as 80%.

Why not just use --cov-fail-under or a Codecov flag?

A floor such as pytest-cov's --cov-fail-under=80 lets a pull request drop from 92% to 81% and still pass. Codecov and Coveralls will catch a delta, but they need an account, a token, and an upload of the report. This tool answers the delta question from two files you already have, locally.

Which coverage formats does this work with?

Cobertura XML (coverage.py, pytest-cov --cov-report=xml, nyc/Istanbul --reporter=cobertura) and JaCoCo XML. Those are the reports most CI jobs already write. LCOV is not read yet.

Is my coverage report uploaded anywhere?

No. The browser page parses the XML you paste entirely in your own browser and never sends it anywhere. The CLI reads local files and makes no network call at all.

More: why coverage drops on a PR that "didn't touch tests", how this compares to a flat coverage floor like --cov-fail-under, or to Codecov, a hosted, connected alternative with a historical dashboard.

Related: if coverage looks fine but the same tests flip between CI runs, the flaky test finder classifies which tests are flaky versus broken from JUnit XML you paste — nothing uploaded.

Related: if every check fails in a few seconds with an empty body before you look at coverage, first check whether GitHub assigned a runner with the actions runner starvation check — paste the run’s job JSON and it reads runner_id.

vs-a-flat-coverage-floor.html.text:
← Coverage Drop Check

Coverage Drop Check vs. a flat coverage floor

A flat coverage floor — --cov-fail-under=80 in pytest-cov, or an equivalent minimum in any coverage tool — is the default method, because most CI setups already have one: fail the build if the overall percentage is below the line. It catches a project that never had good coverage to begin with. It cannot catch a project walking down from good coverage, one merge at a time, as long as every merge stays above the floor — and it cannot catch one file's tests getting gutted inside a single PR if another file's coverage happens to improve enough to keep the total above the line.

FileBaselineThis PRVerdict
auth.py20/20 lines, 100%4/20 lines, 20%dropped — 80.00 points
utils.py72/80 lines, 90%77/80 lines, 96.25%improved — -6.25 points
Overall92/100, 92%81/100, 81%both above an 80% floor

Against a flat --cov-fail-under=80 floor, both reports pass: 92% clears 80, and so does 81%. Nothing about the floor fails, and nothing about it can even see that auth.py lost 16 of its 20 covered lines — the check only ever looks at the one summed-up number. Pasted into this tool, the same two reports resolve to a real finding: line coverage dropped 11.00 points (92.00% → 81.00%), and auth.py is named as the file that got worse, sorted to the top of the report. utils.py's improvement is exactly what kept the overall number above the floor at all — without it, this PR would have failed on the floor alone and never needed a per-file breakdown to catch.

QuestionWhere to answer it
My CI's coverage floor passed — did this PR still make coverage worse? Coverage Drop Check — a floor only checks the absolute number; this checks the direction and names which file moved.
Which specific file's tests got weaker in this PR? Coverage Drop Check — the per-file table sorts dropped files first; a flat floor has no per-file breakdown at all.
This project has never had good test coverage and I want a baseline minimum enforced. A flat floor — that is exactly the job it is built for, and this tool needs a baseline report to compare against, not just an absolute minimum.
Coverage dropped a little on this PR but stayed comfortably above our floor — is that worth blocking on? Neither tool decides that for you. Coverage Drop Check reports the exact points-and-file delta so a reviewer can judge it; a floor cannot even show the number moved.

Neither method is wrong on its own: a floor is the right guard against a codebase that never had coverage discipline, and this tool needs a real baseline report to compare against, which a brand-new project does not have yet. The gap is the case a floor is structurally unable to close — a number that stays technically fine while the file it actually matters for gets worse underneath it, masked by whatever else moved in the same report. That is exactly the gap this tool exists to close.

Common questions

What does a flat coverage floor get wrong?

A floor like --cov-fail-under=80 asks one question: is the overall percentage still above 80? It cannot see direction or which file moved, only where the number sits right now. A PR can walk coverage down from 92% to 81%, one point at a time across many merges, and never once fail the floor — and within a single PR, one file's tests can be gutted while another file's coverage happens to improve enough that the overall percentage still clears 80, so the floor reports a clean pass while a real regression ships inside it.

Can you give a concrete example?

A baseline report shows 92% overall (auth.py fully covered at 100%, utils.py at 90%). After a PR, the report shows 81% overall — auth.py dropped to 20% covered (16 of its 20 lines lost their tests), while utils.py improved slightly to 96.25%, which is what keeps the overall number above an 80% floor at all. A flat --cov-fail-under=80 check passes on both reports: 92 and 81 are each above 80. Pasted into this tool, the same two reports report a real finding: line coverage dropped 11.00 points (92.00% → 81.00%), and auth.py is named as the one file that got worse — the fact the floor has no way to express.

Is this tool just automating something obvious?

Noticing that one file's coverage fell is obvious once you already know to compare that specific file's line rate across the two reports, file by file. What a flat floor gets wrong is that it collapses every file into one number before you ever see it, and a codebase with dozens or hundreds of files makes re-deriving the per-file delta from two raw XML reports exactly the kind of bookkeeping nobody does by hand on every PR. This tool does that comparison mechanically and exhaustively, so a drop hiding behind an improvement elsewhere in the same report does not depend on someone happening to open the one file that got worse.

Does this replace setting a coverage floor?

No. A floor still catches the case this tool cannot: a project that never had good coverage in the first place, or a brand-new file added with no tests and no baseline to compare against. The two catch different failures — a floor bounds the absolute number, this tool bounds the direction and names the file, and neither replaces reading the diff for why a file's tests changed at all.

vs-codecov.html.text:
← Coverage Drop Check

Coverage Drop Check vs. Codecov

Codecov is a hosted coverage service. A GitHub Action (or another CI integration) uploads your coverage report to Codecov's servers on every build. Public repositories on GitHub Actions can upload without a token; private repositories need one, or the newer OIDC-based authentication. Once connected, Codecov keeps a historical dashboard across every branch and contributor, posts a PR comment, and can fail a check on two different signals — codecov/patch (coverage of the lines this PR touched) and codecov/project (overall coverage) — configured through an optional codecov.yml file.

That is a genuinely useful job for a team that wants it running on every build without thinking about it, and it is not this tool's job. This page parses the two coverage XML reports you paste — nothing is uploaded, there is no account, and nothing is remembered once you close the tab.

QuestionWhere to answer it
I have a baseline report and this PR's report right now — did line coverage drop? Coverage Drop Check — paste both, get the percentage-point delta and which files moved, no signup, nothing leaves your device.
I want a coverage status check and PR comment on every build, automatically, for the whole team. Codecov — that needs an ongoing CI integration and an uploaded report on every run, which a stateless browser page never does.
I want historical coverage trends across branches and contributors, or a badge for my README. Codecov's dashboard — this tool has no memory between visits and nowhere to keep history.
My CI already writes coverage.xml or jacoco.xml and I don't want to connect an account or upload it just to check one PR. Coverage Drop Check — the browser page never makes a network request, and the CLI never phones home either.

The two are not substitutes. A team that wants an always-on, connected, historical coverage dashboard with PR comments across every repository needs a hosted tool like Codecov — a page that only looks at whatever you paste into it, once, cannot do that job. A person who already has a baseline report and a PR report and wants the delta before signing up for anything, or without sending code-coverage data to a third party at all, does not need an account or a CI integration to get it.

Common questions

Should I use Coverage Drop Check or Codecov?

They answer a similar question — did coverage get worse — for different situations. Codecov is a hosted service: a GitHub Action (or other CI integration) uploads your coverage report to Codecov's servers on every build, where it is stored, shown on a historical dashboard, and used to post codecov/patch and codecov/project status checks plus a PR comment, across every branch and contributor, continuously, once it is connected. Coverage Drop Check is a free tool with no account and no connection: you paste the baseline report and the current report you already have and get a deterministic percentage-point delta and a per-file breakdown in your browser, right now, with nothing sent anywhere. It answers "did this specific PR drop coverage compared to this specific baseline", once, for whoever is looking at two XML files this minute. If you want an always-on team dashboard with history and PR comments wired into every build, Codecov's job is not one this page tries to do. If you have two reports in hand and want the delta before signing up for anything, that is what this tool is for.

Does using Coverage Drop Check require connecting my CI or creating an account?

No. There is nothing to connect and nothing to sign up for. The browser page parses the XML you paste entirely on your own device and never sends it anywhere; the CLI reads local files and makes no network call at all. Codecov's own public documentation describes the opposite model: its GitHub Action uploads your coverage report to Codecov's servers on every run so the dashboard and status checks can work, and while public repositories on GitHub Actions can upload without a token, using it at all still means creating a Codecov account, installing its GitHub App or Action, and sending your coverage report to Codecov's infrastructure on every build.

Does Codecov do anything this tool cannot?

Yes — a persistent historical dashboard across every build and contributor, native PR comments and commit statuses wired directly into GitHub without pasting anything by hand, coverage badges, support for many more report formats through its universal uploader (LCOV and Clover included, where this tool reads only Cobertura and JaCoCo), and team-wide visibility across many repositories at once. None of that is possible from a page with no server, no account and no memory between visits. This tool only ever computes the delta between the two specific reports you paste into it in that session.

Is this page affiliated with Codecov?

No. This site is not affiliated with, endorsed by, or sponsored by Codecov, Inc. Codecov is named here only to describe what this tool is and is not, based on Codecov's own public documentation.

why-did-my-pr-drop-coverage.html.text:
COVERAGE DROP CHECK · GUIDE

Why did my PR drop coverage when I didn't touch tests?

Coverage is a ratio, not a count of tests. A pull request can lower the number without deleting a single assertion — see the first question below for the arithmetic, then the file list for which modules actually moved.

See the delta first

Guessing from the overall percentage wastes time writing tests in the wrong file. Compare the coverage XML from main against the one from this PR and let the file list tell you — free, runs in your browser, nothing uploaded.

Open Coverage Drop Check →

Common questions

How can coverage drop if I didn't delete any tests?

Coverage is covered lines divided by executable lines. Adding a new branch, a new file, or a refactor that introduces executable lines you did not test increases the denominator. The tests you already had still pass; the rate still falls.

Why did --cov-fail-under=80 still pass after a big drop?

A floor only asks whether the current number is above a threshold. A drop from 92% to 81% is 11 points and still above 80, so the floor stays green. A delta check against a baseline report is what catches that.

Does deleting a well-tested file raise or lower coverage?

It can go either way. Removing a 100%-covered module raises the overall rate if the remaining code was worse; removing a poorly covered module lowers the rate. The file list on a delta report is what tells you which happened, not the single overall number.

How do I see which files actually dropped before I start writing tests?

Keep the coverage XML from main (or the last release) and produce one from the pull request, then compare them. The free Coverage Drop Check tool on this site does that from Cobertura or JaCoCo reports you already have, with no signup and nothing uploaded.

The four changes that move the number most often

1. New untested branches on an existing file

An extra if, an error path, or a feature flag adds executable lines. Existing tests still hit the old path, so they stay green, and the file's rate falls. This is the most common "I didn't touch tests" drop.

2. A new file with no tests yet

A new module starts at 0% unless you added tests in the same PR. The overall rate drops in proportion to how large the file is, even when every previously covered file is unchanged.

3. A refactor that rewrites executable lines

Extracting a helper, inlining a function, or moving code between files can change which lines the same tests hit. The behaviour is identical; the coverage map is not. Compare the file list before assuming tests are missing.

4. A floor check that hid a previous drop

--cov-fail-under and similar gates only fire at a threshold. A series of small PRs can walk coverage from 94% to 81% one point at a time without any of them failing the floor. A delta against main on every PR stops that walk.
